briefOverview: Jeremiah is beaten and imprisoned by the temple official Pashur; God pronounces doom on Pashur while Jeremiah records his anguished mixture of complaint, compelled prophecy, and imprecatory lament.
summary: Pashur, a chief temple official, has Jeremiah beaten and placed in the stocks (1–2). Jeremiah prophesies that Pashur's name will be changed to Magor-missabib ("terror on every side") and announces that Pashur, his household, and the treasures of Judah will be given to the Babylonians (3–6). Jeremiah then pours out an intensely personal lament: he feels deceived by God, is mocked and persecuted, and struggles not to speak God's word even though it is like a "burning fire" in his bones (7–10). He nevertheless affirms that the LORD stands with him and will vindicate him, and he asks God to pour out judgment on his opponents (11–13). The chapter closes with a bitter, poetic curse on the day of his birth, expressing the prophet's deep sorrow and sense of shame (14–18).
externalContext: Jeremiah ministered in late-7th/early-6th century BCE Judah during the rise of Babylon; tensions between prophetic calls to submit to Babylon and popular/political resistance made prophets targets of official opposition. Temple officers like Pashur had both religious and political authority, and public humiliation in stocks (pillory) was a known means of punishment and shaming in the ancient Near East.
externalReferences: The theme of prophetic opposition and plots against Jeremiah appears elsewhere in the book (e.g., Jeremiah 11:19; 26:11) and his later imprisonment is narrated in Jeremiah 38:6. The image of God's word as consuming fire is echoed elsewhere in Jeremiah (23:29). Jeremiah's curse on the day of his birth resembles Job's curse of his birthday (Job 3:1–10) in tone and imagery.
practicalQuestions: How should people today speak truth in public when facing personal cost or official opposition?
When we feel betrayed or 'deceived' by God, how can we hold both our honest complaint and trust in God's justice?
What role does lament (including strong imprecatory language) have in communal and personal spiritual life?
How can communities protect prophets, whistleblowers, or truth-tellers from abuse and public shaming?
uncertainAreas: The tone behind "thou hast deceived me" is ambiguous—whether Jeremiah means genuine deception, a metaphor for unbearable burden, or rhetorical protest. The precise identity of Pashur and the nuances of the name-change (Magor-missabib) have scholarly debate. Some imagery (e.g., wish that his mother had been his grave) may be hyperbolic poetic lament rather than literal suicidal intent.
